newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris stocks cautious even after Juppe resignation.
newsitem.headline: Paris stocks cautious even after Juppe resignation.

text.p: French stock market professionals welcomed news on Monday that Prime Minister Alain Juppe intended to resign but feared fresh falls when London and New York reopen for business after a three-day weekend.
Juppe announced he planned to stand down whatever the outcome of next Sunday's runoff parliamentary vote, in a last-minute bid to save the centre-right's election hopes.

But traders are braced for another tough session after the blue-chip CAC 40 index closed on Monday down 108.16 points, or 3.91 percent, at 2,654.74, following shock gains by the left over the conservative coalition in the first ballot.
"There is a risk the stockmarket will continue to fall tomorrow. The big question is who will buy at the moment. There are no buyers," said Pascal Nigen, equities analyst at GAN.
The market had expected and hoped for Juppe's departure as he was widely unpopular, but the move was unlikely to stop the momentum of the Socialists or the market's fall, he said.
He saw strong support for the CAC index at 2,500 points.
"The British and American reaction tomorrow will be the test. If there's a big selling movement, the market could sell another hundred points," said a trader at a European brokerage.
"But if people remain watchful, we'll stay at these levels."
EIFB technical analyst Pierre Vignaud sees the CAC falling possibly as low as 2,570.

The Socialists are perceived to be more ambiguous on European monetary union and oppose tough reforms to streamlining the French state system, with its generous social benefits, and company restructuring efforts which would cut jobs.
Traders and equities analysts said Juppe was viewed as a liability for the centre-right RPR-UDF coalition. "The real campaign will be launched tonight," a trader said.

"Stepping down seems to be positive news that the government is listening to the message from the electors," said an equity salesman at a big French brokerage. "It will wait and see who's going to replace him," he added.

Joanne Perez, economist at Merrill Lynch said, "The market reaction will depend on who will replace Juppe. It may be (National Assembly speaker) Philippe Seguin, who is a popular choice but not the market's choice. He is ambiguous on Maastricht, pro-growth and less rigorous on public deficits."
On the more liberal path there is former prime minister Edouard Balladur or former budget minister Nicolas Sarkozy, both of whom would be more positive for the markets.
But perceived as most positive is former finance minister Alain Madelin, the most pro-business of the liberals.
"It's an important strategic choice by the right to determine whether to go for market liberal policies and free-entreprise or reassure social protection will be maintained," she said.

The CAC May futures contract traded at 2,656 on the GLOBEX electronic trading system at 1720 GMT, after a brief run up of 12 points on the Juppe resignation news. At its present level, it is down 106 points from Friday.
The CAC had gained nearly 20 percent so far this year and 10 percent since the elections were announced a month ago as investors bet that the conservatives would win handily.
